mcqs.question: What actually distinguishes a "suspended" app from a "background" app in the four-state model?
options: Suspended apps are still running code at reduced priority
A suspended process is frozen in memory with no code executing, while a background process is still actively running within a budget
Suspended apps have already been removed from memory
There is no real difference; the terms are used interchangeably across platforms
mcqs.explanation: Background means the process is alive and executing (within a limited budget); suspended means the OS has frozen it entirely as a memory snapshot — nothing runs until it's foregrounded again or killed. Removing it from memory is the next state down, killed.

mcqs.question: Why does a mobile OS kill background processes without notifying the app first?
options: It's a bug that platform vendors have not yet fixed
Because memory and battery are scarce, and giving every background app a graceful shutdown window would defeat the point of reclaiming resources quickly
Notifications are sent, but most apps ignore them
Only apps that crash are terminated this way
mcqs.explanation: The kill exists precisely to free memory fast for the foreground app; a mandatory grace period would undercut that goal, so the OS reclaims first and lets the app discover it on next launch. This is deliberate design, not a defect, and it applies to well-behaved apps too.

mcqs.question: An app starts a long-running network sync right as the user backgrounds it. What should it do?
options: Nothing — background execution budgets are unlimited as long as the app was recently foregrounded
Assume the OS will pause and later resume the sync exactly where it left off
Recognize the background execution budget is short, and either finish quickly, checkpoint progress, or request an explicit background-task extension
Convert the sync into a foreground-only operation that blocks the UI thread
mcqs.explanation: Backgrounding shrinks the execution budget to a short window; work that can't finish in it must checkpoint or explicitly request extended background execution, which the OS can still revoke. There's no implicit unlimited budget and no guaranteed resume-in-place.

mcqs.question: A user switches away from your app for ten seconds, then switches back, and the app reappears instantly with no rebuild. What kind of start just happened?
options: Cold start, because the OS always tears down the process after backgrounding
Warm start, because the process survived but the UI had to be recreated
Hot start, because the process and its UI were both still alive in memory and simply resumed
This scenario is not one of the three recognized start types
mcqs.explanation: A ten-second background is well within typical suspension windows, so both process and UI usually survive — that's a hot start, resuming straight from memory with no rebuild work. Warm start still requires recreating the UI; cold start requires spawning a new process entirely.

mcqs.question: Which of these reliably survives your app's process being killed by the OS?
options: A row you already committed to an on-device database before backgrounding
A value held only in a ViewModel or equivalent in-memory holder
An open network socket that was mid-request
A static singleton's cached value
mcqs.explanation: Anything written to durable storage before the kill survives, because a kill only wipes process memory, not disk. In-memory holders, open sockets, and static caches all live in that reclaimed process memory and are gone with it.

mcqs.question: Why does state-restoration breakage often ship undetected through an entire release cycle?
options: Because state restoration is optional on most platforms and rarely required
Because QA teams are not permitted to test lifecycle behavior
Because development devices have far more RAM than typical user devices and rarely reach the memory pressure that triggers a kill, so the bug never appears in normal dev testing
Because the OS guarantees restoration will always work correctly
mcqs.explanation: Dev phones with light app load and high RAM rarely hit the memory pressure that kills backgrounded apps, so restoration code paths simply never execute during normal testing — the fix is to force-kill the process deliberately as part of the test pass, which both major platforms support.
